title: Topic Exchange: Flexible Routing with Wildcards
description: Master topic exchanges and wildcard-based routing for flexible, scalable message distribution.

data.text: A **topic exchange** routes messages to queues based on pattern matching between the message's routing key and the patterns specified when binding queues. Routing keys consist of words separated by dots (e.g., `order.created.us`), and binding patterns support two wildcards: `*` matches exactly one word, and `#` matches one or more words.

The `*` wildcard matches a single word in any position. So `order.*` matches `order.created` but not `order.created.us`. The `#` wildcard matches zero or more words — `order.#` matches `order.created`, `order.created.us`, and even just `order`. Combining wildcards gives you powerful expressive routing patterns.

data.caption: Topic exchange routing keys matched against binding patterns
data.definition:
graph TD
    P[Publisher] --> E[topic: app.events]
    E -->|key: user.signup| Q1[pattern: user.*]
    E -->|key: order.created| Q2[pattern: order.#]
    E -->|key: payment.failed| Q3[pattern: *.failed]
    Q1 --> C1[Consumer: UserService]
    Q2 --> C2[Consumer: OrderService]
    Q3 --> C3[Consumer: Alerting]

data.text: Topic exchanges shine when you need category- and subcategory-based routing. For example, an e-commerce system might use routing keys like `order.created.us`, `order.cancelled.eu`, and `payment.failed.global`. Binding queues with patterns like `order.#` lets the order service listen to all order events regardless of region, while `*.failed` routes all failure events to a centralized alerting service.

Kafka's topic model follows the same conceptual pattern: each topic functions like a log, and consumer groups subscribe to one or more topics. While Kafka does not support pattern-based routing within a topic, its topic naming convention achieves the same outcome by encouraging dot-separated hierarchies at the infrastructure level. Understanding topic exchange patterns in RabbitMQ prepares you well for Kafka topic design.

data.title: Avoid Overly Broad Patterns
data.text: Using `#` as a binding pattern means your queue receives every message on the exchange. This can overload consumers and defeat the purpose of message routing. Use the most specific pattern that satisfies your requirements.

terms.definition: An AMQP exchange type that routes messages using pattern matching with wildcards (* and #) against the routing key.
Matches exactly one word in a routing key. For example, order.* matches order.created but not order.created.us.
Matches zero or more words in a routing key. For example, order.# matches order.created, order.created.us, and order.

items.question: Can I use both * and # in the same binding pattern?
items.answer: Yes. Patterns like *.created.# are valid and match any word, then created, then any remaining words. This gives you maximum flexibility in routing.

items.question: Does Kafka support wildcard topic subscriptions natively?
items.answer: No. Kafka requires explicit topic names in consumer subscriptions. Wildcard behavior must be implemented at the application level using topic pattern regex subscriptions available since Kafka 2.2.0.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Topic exchanges use wildcards (* for one word, # for zero or more words) to match routing keys.
Multiple queues can receive the same message if their binding patterns match.
Use the most specific pattern possible to avoid unnecessary message delivery.
Topic exchanges are the most flexible and widely used exchange type.

data.title: Exercise: Design a Topic Routing Scheme
data.description: Design a topic exchange routing scheme for a multi-tenant SaaS notification platform. You need to support: (1) email notifications per tenant, (2) SMS notifications per tenant, (3) push notifications per tenant, (4) all notifications for a given priority (low, medium, high), and (5) a dead-letter audit queue that captures every notification.
steps: List the queues and their binding patterns
Show which queues receive a message with key: email.tenant42.high
Show which queues receive a message with key: sms.tenant99.low
data.expectedOutcome: A clear table of routing key format, queue names, binding patterns, and example match results.
